sentences: Renowned psychiatrist and criminologist the doctor, the "crime specialist", is called on an emergency to a party at his next door neighbor, where a man, the victim, suffers from a diabetic seizure and has collapsed on the floor.
The doctor administers insulin to the man, using the man's own case, but a short while after the injection is made the man dies.
Suspecting something out of the ordinary, the doctor calls on his friend, the inspector, who works in the homicide division.
The inspector concludes that the man was poisoned.
The doctor's services are used to aid in the investigation, and he gets a list of the guests at the party.
He starts questioning them, one by one, beginning with the dead man's sister, the young woman.
She tells him she has no clue to what her brother meant by his last words: "I've given you one face."
Next is the young woman's lover, the boyfriend, owner of a health institute.
He and the victim did not get along well, and the victim was opposed to him marrying his sister.
The boyfriend also tells the doctor that the victim had financial problems, and the doctor pays a visit to the attorney who handled the victim's affairs, the lawyer.
He learns that the victim had spent most of what he had inherited from his father and also wanted to borrow money from his sister.
The young woman calls the doctor and asks him to come to her apartment right away.
Apparently he doesn't get there fast enough, since he finds the home empty and the young woman has been kidnapped (by the henchman).
The doctor goes on to investigate both the murder and the kidnapping.
When he visits his neighbor the hostess, she reveals that she and her husband are selling the house, giving as reason that they cannot stay in a house where a murder took place.
The doctor talks to her real estate agent, the realtor, to have this information confirmed.
The realtor confirms the sale but states the true reason: they are divorcing.
Later in the day he gets a visit from the informant, who tells him all about the hostess's romantic involvement with the victim.
According to the informant, the hostess had given the victim money from her own account.
The informant ends with telling the doctor about the other woman the victim was seeing, the mistress, who works at a mortuary.
After many phone calls, the doctor finds out the mortuary where the mistress works.
He calls and sets up a meeting with her, but the mistress is locked into a room at her office by one of the other employees.
The person trapping her is the henchman, who suspects that the mistress is involved in a scam to blackmail the owner of the mortuary, the mortician.
The henchman goes to visit the doctor, posing as a man who is concerned about his brother the gunman's mental health.
As soon as the henchman and the gunman enter the doctor's office, the gunman shoots the doctor in the head.
The doctor's vision is impaired but he is not seriously wounded.
After the shot, the henchman pushes the gunman out through the window, where he plunges to his death.
Since there are no fingerprints after the henchman's visit, the doctor suspects that a plastic surgeon might be involved.
The doctor gets his eyesight back, but pretends to be still blind.
Looking at criminal records, he manages to match the signature he got from the henchman with the gangster, a hardened criminal, who must have had plastic surgery to change his facial features.
The doctor poses as a criminal himself, the outlaw, to get close to the gangster.
He tells the gangster he wants to change his appearance and is sent to the mortician's mortuary.
Before the doctor arrives, the gangster hears a news report on the radio that notorious criminal the outlaw is dead, and calls the mortician ahead to warn him.
When the doctor arrives to the mortuary, the mortician tries to poison him with an injection, but the doctor manages to break free and knock out the mortician.
The police arrive to arrest both the mortician and the gangster, and both the young woman and the mistress are found dead in the localities.
Still the head of the criminal operation, the plastic surgeon, seems to be on the loose.
All the remaining suspects are invited to a party at the doctor's house, where he continues to pretend he is blind.
After all the other guests have gone, the realtor comes back and says he has forgotten his glasses.
He spikes a drink for the doctor with poison and waits for the doctor to swallow it.
Then he confesses to the doctor that he killed the victim because the victim had knowledge about the realtor's past as a surgeon.
In an art gallery, the drama critic sees a portrait of a beautiful woman painted by the artist [an actor], gazing at it, entranced.
He asks the gallery owner who the model was; the owner says that it was the artist's only model and is not for sale.
Puzzled, the critic returns to his office; he knows the face but cannot remember her name.
He phones the artist with a proposal to buy the painting, but the artist refuses.
The critic continues his pursuit to find out who the model for the painting was.
He learns her name is the singer (an actress), but the young woman looks nothing like the woman in the painting.
He visits with her to learn the artist's location, but she refuses, telling him that she will be singing at a local nightclub which the artist frequents.
The critic confronts the artist there, while the artist is sketching a stabbing, with what he has remembered of the artist being accused of murdering his first model, the earlier victim.
The artist is adamant that he was completely exonerated of her murder.
Becoming clearly annoyed, the artist invites the singer out for a night in his yacht.
She agrees, but her body is later found washed ashore.
Although the police lieutenant initially questions the singer's suitor, the admirer, the admirer implicates the artist as the last person who saw the singer.
The critic works with the police department to arrange for the singer's sister, the new model (a second actress), to apply for modeling, in order to spy on the artist.
The two return to the artist's boathouse.
While there, the new model calls for the critic and tells his chef that she is in danger and to notify the police.

She is suspicious of the artist when he acts moodily, when he plays "weird and strange" improvised music on the piano, when he throws away her tiny revolver she brought in her purse for protection, and again when he mixes drinks for the two of them.
But when the artist drinks her drink rather than let it go to waste, she knows for certain he is not plotting anything against her.
Another wealthy woman, the socialite (a third actress) tries twice to buy the artist's art, but he refuses.
Since the artist is convinced the new model was only around to spy on him, he strikes up a flirtatious friendship with the socialite.
When the socialite tells the new model she is going to marry the artist, the new model angrily congratulates the socialite and hurriedly leaves in tears.
But the socialite is turned down by the artist when she proposes marriage.
She tells the artist he will end up with the new model.
The artist leaves the socialite in her car, and when the socialite returns home, she receives a phone call from someone who invites her to go back to the artist's boathouse.
When she arrives at the door, the curtains are suddenly drawn.
Back in his own apartment/studio, the artist lies down on a couch, exhausted, and has a dream of kissing the singer, who suddenly screams and falls into the water, disappearing in the darkness.
Then he dreams of the earlier victim, but when he kisses her, she also screams and falls into the water and darkness.
The new model awakens the artist, who is distraught but explains he made the other women die, and there are some things so fearful the mind rejects them.
The new model tells him it is only a dream.
He tells her she needs to go away, and the new model replies that since he is getting married, his wife can model for him.
He tells the new model he has seen the socialite for the last time.
As they kiss, they are interrupted by the police, who are looking for the socialite, whose car was found abandoned.
The police hold the artist for questioning and tell him the socialite was murdered in the same way as the other women.
The artist seems confused and doubts his memory.
The new model and the artist's mother come to the district attorney's office.
The D.A. is convinced that the artist is refusing to confess and asks the new model to convince him.
But the new model tells the artist not to confess.
The district attorney holds up a piece of fur that was torn from the socialite's dress, which was found in his boathouse.
The artist continues to say he is confused, and the new model persists in saying she will fight for him, because she believes in him.
The new model returns home with the artist's mother, who first tells the new model to lie down on a couch due to having a headache.
The artist's mother sounds sympathetic and shares how she also has headaches which "almost drive me mad."
The examiner administers lie detector tests for the district attorney, her boss, but wants to become a prosecutor in court.
Frustrated, she leaves her boss to work for the lawyer, whose unhappy wife, a photographer, makes large bets with the bookie and openly flirts with the model's husband.
Her boss is in love with the examiner and wants her back.
He fools the lawyer into believing the wife wants to reconcile, but instead the other man turns up, telling the lawyer he and the wife have become romantically involved.
The wife then is found dead.
Her boss and the police naturally suspect the lawyer.
The bookie refuses to pay the $20,000 that the wife won with her bet.
The model is then killed.
At a party, the examiner convinces her guests to take one of her lie detector tests.
From the answers she gets, she deduces that the other man is the killer behind it all.
She is saved from being his next victim by her boss, with whom she is now in love.
The detective (an actor) is a private investigator living in the city.
One day a Chinese princess comes to visit him in his home.
She has just arrived from the East by boat.
The princess manages to give the detective’s butler (an actor) an artifact - an ancient heirloom ring - before she is shot and killed by a poisoned arrow through the window.
She leaves a note behind, with the name ”a captain's initial”.
The detective calls for the police to investigate this murder.
The policeman (an actor) with the city police comes to the detective, but his friend, the reporter (an actress), also arrives uninvited to the scene.
By examining the ring, it turns out the princess’ name was her full name (an actress).
She arrived in the city weeks earlier with two men, the first captain (an actor) and the second captain (an actor), to try to acquire fighter planes to fight off an enemy back home.
For this purpose she had brought a substantial amount of money, $1,000,000, with her on the journey.
A search for the money ensues, but it soon turns out there are more people looking for the lost money.
The reporter helps out in the hunt, and she meets the princess’ maid (an actress), and a deaf-mute boy living in the princess' apartment.

When the detective comes to talk to the maid, he finds her murdered in the apartment, and the deaf-mute boy manages to tell him that a man came to visit the apartment shortly before the maid was found dead.
The detective continues his search for the money, visiting the banker (who reads and writes in fluent Chinese) in charge of handling the princess’ assets abroad (an actor).
While they are talking, the first captain and the second captain, eager to get their share of the money, break in and kidnap both men and hold them for ransom.
They are taken to the Chinese cargo vessel, but the butler manages to track them to the ship.

Together with the detective’s son (an actor), they manage to free the detective and the banker, and when the policeman and the reporter arrive to the ship with the police, the first captain and the second captain are captured and arrested.
The detective discovers that the banker is guilty of the princess’ murder, and of stealing her money.
The banker also killed the maid to cover his tracks, and then killed the little deaf-mute Chinese boy and buried him secretly in a pet cemetery plot to hide the crime.

In 1947, the inspector of the police headquarters suspects the adventurer, the reformed jewel thief known as the "master thief," is behind the theft of the priceless diamonds called the "famous gems".
The adventurer denies any involvement claiming that he is in the city with his butler, the manservant to write a book on the jewels and was in another city when they were stolen.
The adventurer and the manservant are short of funds and when the young woman, the daughter of the wealthy gem collector, invites them to the family estate, they agree.
The collector confides that he is in desperate need of money and asks the adventurer to arrange a confidential loan with part of his jewel collection as collateral.

The manservant tells his master that the maid told him the family butler is heartbroken because his former wife, the actress, has run off with the backer who financed the lavish stage production that launched the actress to stardom.
Back at his hotel, the adventurer receives a call from the actress, inviting him to the theater that night where she asks him to stay away from the collector's family.
At her apartment, the family butler begs her for a reconciliation, but she demands something first.
The adventurer decides to accept the collector's offer and arranges to meet the dealer, a gem dealer the next morning.
The collector gives the family butler a packet of jewels to deliver to the adventurer but he steals the famous gems for the actress.
The young woman's fiancé asks him for a ride because he wants to spy on the adventurer.
At the dealer's shop, the inspector has followed the adventurer.
When the family butler's car rolls to a stop, the butler is dead behind the wheel, the jewels still in his possession but the famous gems are gone.
The fiancé claims the family butler pushed him out of the car on the outskirts, and said he suspects the adventurer was the murderer.
The adventurer thinks the collector was being blackmailed by the thief who sold him the diamonds, and flees the police and proceeds to the actress' apartment.
She has just persuaded the backer to get the diamonds from the adventurer.
The adventurer and the backer struggle with the backer being subdued and told that the actress was about to flee with the famous master thief.

At the theater, the adventurer discovers the diamonds are sewn into her mink coat but before he can leave her dressing room, the actress enters and admits that the family butler had given her the diamonds.
While the adventurer phones the manservant, the actress sneaks out an open window and heads to the airport to catch a flight out of the country.

At the airport, the adventurer confronts the actress and turns her over to the waiting inspector but the backer arrives, wielding a gun and declaring the actress planned the entire robbery and then killed the family butler for the diamonds.
When the manservant brings the maid and the actress' mink, the adventurer extracts the famous gems from the coat's linings, proving that the actress was the thief and murderer.
Former jewel thief the adventurer (the master thief) (an actor) along with his butler, the manservant (an actor), go to a foreign country on vacation.
The adventurer, once a thief has been working as a private investigator.
The former sweetheart (an actress), one of the master thief's old flames, and the dowager (an actress) invite the adventurer and the manservant to dinner at the club owner's (an actor) nightclub.
They meet the young wife (an actress), a jeweller's spouse and gambling addict, who has lost a fortune at the casino.
The plotter (an actor), the former sweetheart's husband, tries to enlist the adventurer in a jewel theft.
The manservant takes the young wife home, but when he is not looking, she slips a valuable compact into his coat pocket.
After the master thief steals a necklace, he discovers it is a fake and replaces it in the nightclub safe.
When the plotter is murdered, the young wife accuses the adventurer of the murder and the manservant of stealing her compact.
The dowager is also heavily in debt with the club owner demanding her precious necklace to clear her gambling losses.
The young wife blackmails the club owner and tries to warn the adventurer but is also murdered, leaving him no alternative, he must track down the criminal mastermind behind the murders.
The dowager plots with the club owner but her worthless necklace is what gives her away and the adventurer calls in the police to bring the club owner and the dowager, the real murderer to justice.
The detective and the detective's wife are attending a charity ball sponsored by the collector.
The collector and staged aboard the vessel.
The vessel, the ship owner's gambling ship.
The entertainment is provided by a jazz band consisting of the bandleader, the sultry singer, and the talented but unstable clarinetist.
After a set, the bandleader informs a displeased ship owner that he is quitting the band, as the booking agent has booked a tour of dance halls for him.
However, the bandleader owes the gangster $12,000.
When the gangster—who is at the party—hears the news, he demands full payment that night.
The bandleader begs the booking agent to give him an advance, but the booking agent is unwilling to part with such a large sum.
In desperation, the bandleader sneaks into the ship owner's office and opens the safe, when he is shot from behind and killed by an unseen assailant.
The ship owner and the socialite elope, as her father the collector disapproves of the ship owner's lower-class background.
The next morning, they visit the detective and the detective's wife's apartment, having learned that the ship owner is the prime suspect in the murder.
The ship owner and the socialite ask the detective to help them clear their names, but the detective worries that he and the detective's wife may be implicated.
As the detective sees the ship owner and the socialite out, a bullet nearly strikes the ship owner.
The detective turns the ship owner over to the police, convinced that he will be safer in police custody.
The detective then starts investigating.
Sneaking aboard the vessel, the detective discovers on the back of a sheet of music a receipt signed by the gangster acknowledging that the bandleader's debt had been paid.
The detective then runs into the remaining members of the bandleader's band, allowed back on board to collect their instruments.
When he questions them, he learns that the bandleader had many enemies, among them the clarinetist.
The musician agrees to help the detective locate the clarinetist, but they have no luck.

After the detective concludes that the bullet that killed the bandleader was fired from an antique gun, he and the detective's wife visit the socialite and her father the collector, an avid collector of antiques.
The detective finds that one gun is missing from the collector's collection, and the collector tells the detective that the ship owner had the missing gun the night of the murder.
The socialite accuses the collector of lying, and after receiving a mysterious telephone call, she leaves in a hurry.
The detective and the detective's wife follow the socialite to the singer's apartment where they find the singer's body, recently stabbed in the back.
The socialite claims the singer called to sell her some information that would help her prove the ship owner's innocence, but that she arrived after the singer was killed.
A matchbook found in the singer's apartment leads the detective and the detective's wife to a sanatorium in a nearby town, where the clarinetist is undergoing treatment.
The clarinetist is too badly shaken to answer the detective's questions, though the detective's wife's presence seems to calm him down.
When the detective's wife sneaks back later by herself, the clarinetist becomes agitated, confesses to the murder, pulls out the antique gun, and tries to shoot the detective's wife but misses.

The detective does not believe the deranged man's confession as the bandleader was slain by a well-aimed shot, and deduces that the real culprit planted the murder weapon on the clarinetist and that the singer was murdered because she knew who killed the bandleader.
To lure out the killer, the detective gathers all the suspects by throwing a party on the reopened vessel.
The detective's wife notices that the gangster's wife is wearing a valuable necklace that matches the earrings owned by the booking agent's wife.
Soon afterward, the necklace mysteriously reappears on the booking agent's wife's neck.
When the detective confronts the booking agent, the booking agent's wife admits that it was she who paid off her lover the bandleader's debt using the necklace.

As the detective asks a fully recovered clarinetist to reveal the killer's identity, the booking agent confesses to killing the bandleader because of his affair with the booking agent's wife, and also confesses to killing the singer to cover up his crime.
In desperation, the booking agent pulls out a gun, but the booking agent's wife shoots him first and kills him as revenge for the bandleader's murder.

The private detective and his girlfriend/secretary are in the office ready to leave on a duck-hunting vacation but are puzzled when a mysterious stranger arrives who announces that he intended to offer a bribe to not take a certain unspecified case, but hearing that the detective is going away anyway, abruptly departs.
The mystery deepens when the detective is invited over by an informant with an offer to sell certain valuable information which the detective declines.

Leaving the informant's, the detective is ambushed by a pair of odd thugs under orders of their boss seeking to know what the informant told him, which was nothing; they beat up and leave the detective in the city dump.
Now drawn in to an obvious situation, the detective sends his reporter friend to accept the informant's information offer, but instead the reporter friend encounters police and her murdered body.
It turns out that the mystery concerns criminal activity at the local racetrack.
The president's track manager hires the detective to solve a counterfeit ticket racket that is bankrupting the track.
The printer for the legitimate tickets is a trusted company owned by the president, and the track manager alone decides on the tickets' secret daily design and code numbers.
The track offers one other lead.
The publisher, owner of the newspaper, had long been trying to get the contract for printing the tickets.
He had financed the purchase of the newspaper using as collateral a printing company he'd acquired from a prison inmate, a certain convict.
The detective recognizes the publisher as the stranger who offered the bribe to drop the case and he won't answer questions.
The publisher's partner, the photographer/engraver, also refuses to be questioned.
As it turns out, the publisher is aka the certain convict and the engraver is aka another convict.
Years ago they were convicted of together counterfeiting Irish sweepstakes tickets and sent to the penitentiary.
The publisher served a light sentence and was released but the engraver drew 20 to 50 and after two years, broke out.
The engraver has acquired a wife and son who know nothing about his past.

Despite the efforts of the engraver to remake his life, inventing a new type of camera, sadly the track manager figured out his identity and began blackmailing the escaped convict to force him to make the counterfeit racing tickets.
We are now at the point of the film where the track manager fears the engraver will talk and directs his thugs to kill him, as he had ordered the death of the informant who knew about the blackmail.

But just as he speaks this order into the phone, the engraver shows up to instead shoot and kill the track manager; in turn as he is leaving, the engraver is shot and killed by the track manager's thugs.
At the end, one thug reveals the other, the second thug, as the killer of the informant and the engraver; the second thug attacks and is shot by the other as police arrive and capture him.
In the final scene, the police agree at the detective's request to spare the engraver's family from the truth, and the detective and his girlfriend/secretary at last embark on their vacation.
The stern judge, a principled but stubborn judge, presides over a murder case in which the lawyer is unsuccessful in proving that his client's state of mind was a mitigating factor.
The stern judge's daughter complains to her mother about how unyielding her father can be; the wife insists that he is a loving husband.
Anyway, it is their 20th wedding anniversary and she is planning to celebrate with friends at their house.
The stern judge does not know that the daughter (herself a law student) and the lawyer are romantically involved until the lawyer arrives during the party to take her on a date.
The stern judge and the lawyer exchange sharp words of disagreement about their philosophies of the law.
At the party, the wife talks to the doctor, an expert neurologist and friend of the family, about her intermittent symptoms of weakness and headaches.
At his office, the doctor performs a series of tests and then consults other experts.
Rather than tell her the truth, the doctor contacts her husband.
The wife has an inoperable brain tumor and will suffer increasingly until it kills her.
The stern judge agrees, rather than spoiling her remaining days, to keep the information secret.
The doctor gives him a bottle of pills called the strong drug for pain relief, strongly warning him about the maximum dosage, and a prescription for more.
The stern judge, who previously said he was too busy with cases to take the wife on a second honeymoon as she wished, now agrees to go at once.
But her condition worsens rapidly, including excruciatingly painful headaches.
The stern judge gives her a dose of the strong drug, pretending it is aspirin.
While he is calling the doctor from a pay phone so the wife will not hear, a dog is run over in the street, and a police officer ends its suffering with a gunshot.
The stern judge, evidently feeling disgust at similar thoughts of his own, discards the remaining pills.
The wife, looking through their luggage for toiletries, accidentally discovers the doctor's written diagnosis and prescription.
When the stern judge returns to the room, she says she is feeling better but would like to return home.
In the car, her symptoms return.
They stop at a gas station to have a car problem repaired and the stern judge asks urgently about the nearest drugstore.
Back on the road, the wife collapses in the car.
The stern judge can stand it no more.
He deliberately drives off an embankment, not caring if he is also killed.
He survives, confesses that he crashed on purpose, and in keeping with his philosophy, demands to be prosecuted for murder.
At the daughter's request, the lawyer agrees to defend the stern judge.
He requests an autopsy in case the wife had actually died from her illness before the crash.
The finding is a surprise: she did die before the crash, but from a strong drug overdose.
The lawyer shows that she had had the prescription filled before the drive home, and taken the drug while at the gas station.
The trial judge then dismisses the murder charge, but declares that the stern judge knew very well that what he tried to do was wrong, and should consider himself morally guilty.

The stern judge agrees, and announces that in expiation, if allowed to remain a judge, he will now rule on the basis that similarly a person can be legally guilty but morally innocent—just what the lawyer and the daughter have been asking for.
The mine owner, owner of the gold mine in a western state, persuades the detective to help him.
To avoid alerting the mine owner's murderous enemies, the detective registers as a guest at a nearby dude ranch along with his number two son, and his black chauffeur.
There he meets the big-city police lieutenant, posing as drunken fellow guest "an assumed name" to investigate why the mine has suddenly become valuable.
When the detective goes to see the mine owner, he finds that he has supposedly fallen down a mineshaft, leaving him in a coma.
While there, he is recognized by the assayer, who knows him from a previous case.
Later, the detective guesses that the prospector is stealing ore from the mine.
The prospector agrees to guide the detective, the son, and the chauffeur to the mine through his secret passageway.
However, when they arrive, the son and the chauffeur find the prospector's body.
The detective eventually surmises that much cheaper Mexican gold is being smuggled into the country and sold at a huge profit.
The detective exposes the ringleader and his confederates.
